sections.title: A shirt found among rags
sections.intro_md:
In 1977 conservators at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London were sorting a bundle of what had been filed as **funerary rags** from an Egyptian cemetery. One lump of crumpled linen turned out to be a shirt, with sleeves, a neckline and fine pleats still pressed into the cloth.

Flinders Petrie had dug it up at **Tarkhan**, south of Cairo, in 1913, and it had sat unexamined for 65 years. In 2015 an Oxford radiocarbon test put the linen between **3482 and 3102 BC**. That makes it the oldest woven garment known anywhere, older than the pyramids, older than writing in most of the world.

That shirt is the right place to start, because it breaks the picture most of us carry of ancient Egypt: stiff white kilts and clinging sheaths, exactly as the tomb paintings show. Real Egyptian clothes were baggier, more varied and more personal. And across the desert in Mesopotamia, people dressed in something quite different: sheep. Today is about what two of the first civilisations actually wore, how we know, and why it still shapes how we dress.

spotlights.name: The Tarkhan dress
spotlights.spot_it: A small, crumpled V-necked linen shirt with pleated sleeves, mounted flat in a glass case in London.
spotlights.story_md: Petrie found it outside a mastaba tomb at **Tarkhan** in 1913, among discarded linens. It went to University College London and was forgotten. In 1977 conservators at the **Victoria and Albert Museum** found it while sorting 'funerary rags', turned it right side out and saw a garment. The body is a straight piece of cloth about **76 cm** wide, with 22 to 23 warp threads per centimetre. The hem is missing, so nobody knows if it was a shirt or a full-length dress. A 1978 test said about 2362 BC. A 2015 Oxford test pushed it back to **3482 to 3102 BC**. Creases at the elbows suggest someone wore it in life.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the oldest woven garment known, made before Egypt was even a single kingdom.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's oldest shirt spent 65 years filed as a rag.

sections.title: Two rivers, two wardrobes
sections.intro_md:
Egypt and Mesopotamia grew up at the same time, about 3500 to 3000 BC, a thousand kilometres apart. Both were river civilisations. Both had kings, scribes, temples and huge workforces. Yet they dressed from different animals and plants.

**Egypt dressed in linen.** Flax grew in the Nile's mud, and linen is cool, light and takes a crisp pleat. Wool was used, but less, and Herodotus says it was barred from temples and graves.

**Mesopotamia dressed in wool.** The plains between the Tigris and Euphrates fed enormous flocks of sheep. Early Sumerians wore the fleece itself, then wove wool into tufted skirts, long fringed shawls and, much later, the heavy embroidered robes of Assyrian kings.

spotlights.name: Flax, the plant behind linen
spotlights.when: Woven in Egypt from c. 5600 to 4400 BC (Faiyum A)
spotlights.spot_it: A thin plant knee to waist high with small sky-blue flowers; in tomb paintings, workers pull it up by the roots in bundles.
spotlights.story_md: Linen comes from the stalk, not the flower. Egyptians **pulled** flax out of the ground rather than cutting it, so the fibre ran the full length of the stem. The stalks were soaked to rot away the soft parts, beaten, combed and then spun. Young green flax gave the finest thread; older yellow stalks gave coarse, strong yarn for rope and sacks. The earliest weaving in Egypt dates from the **Faiyum A** farmers, about 5600 to 4400 BC. Dyed flax fibres from a cave in Georgia are about 36,000 years old, so humans had been twisting this plant into thread for a very long time before anyone built a pyramid.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Almost every piece of Egyptian clothing, bandage and mummy wrapping started as this plant.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egypt's whole wardrobe grew in mud and had blue flowers.

sections.title: Making cloth: the first big industry
sections.intro_md:
Before anyone could get dressed, someone had to spin. Every metre of cloth in the ancient world began as fibre twisted into thread on a **spindle**, often by women working for hours a day. Weaving came next, on a loom pegged out flat on the ground in Egypt, or on looms that later stood upright.

This was not a cottage hobby. In both civilisations cloth was wealth. It paid wages, filled temple storerooms, wrapped the dead and travelled as trade goods. In southern Mesopotamia around 2100 BC, one state office in Girsu oversaw roughly **6,000** textile workers, mostly women and children, paid in rations and tracked on clay tablets that record working days and how long each piece took. A few centuries later, families in the city of Ashur were sending woollen cloth by donkey caravan to Anatolia and getting silver back.

The spotlights below show the tools, the workshops and the paperwork.

pins.label: Thebes and the Valley of the Kings

spotlights.name: Meketre's weaving workshop model

where.label: Tomb TT280, Thebes; now Met Museum and Cairo

spotlights.spot_it: A painted wooden box room the size of a shoebox, full of tiny women spinning thread and working two flat looms on the floor.
spotlights.story_md: The official **Meketre** was buried at Thebes with a set of painted wooden models of daily life: a granary, a butcher's shop, boats, a garden, and a weaving room. Archaeologists split the models between New York's Metropolitan Museum and the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. In models and paintings of this kind, women sit on the floor beside a **horizontal ground loom**, pegged out flat, while others draw out and twist flax into thread. Because the figures are carved in action, the models show steps that a written text would skip, such as how a spinner fed thread from a pot to the spindle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a 3D instruction manual for how Egyptian cloth was made.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dead man took a tiny clothing factory with him.

spotlights.name: Spindle and whorl
spotlights.spot_it: A stick with a round weight near one end; spun like a top, it twists fibre into thread.
spotlights.story_md: Spinning was the slowest step in making cloth, and almost every adult woman did it. The **whorl**, a weight of stone, clay or wood, keeps the spindle turning. Archaeologists love whorls because they survive when cloth does not. At **Mohenjo-daro** in the Indus valley, spindle whorls turn up alongside cotton fragments of the 3rd millennium BC. In Egypt, a dish from the Naqada period in London's Petrie Museum shows a loom, one of the oldest pictures of weaving anywhere. One estimate often quoted by textile historians is that a single linen garment needed many days of spinning, far more than weaving.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Whorls tell us where cloth was made even when every thread has rotted.
spotlights.memory_hook: Before the loom, the top: every thread began as a spin.

spotlights.name: The Ur III textile workshops
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of small clay tablets packed with wedge-shaped signs: the payroll and output of state weaving sheds.
spotlights.story_md: Under the **Third Dynasty of Ur**, textiles were the biggest activity in state workshops. One office in Girsu province oversaw about **6,000 workers**, probably spread across several workshops. Most were women, with children working beside them, and everyone was paid in **rations** of barley, oil and wool. Scribes recorded working days, the kind of cloth produced and how much time each piece took, with startling precision. Weavers could be moved to the harvest, to grinding flour or to hauling boats when the state needed hands. About 120,000 tablets survive from this period, which is why historians know more about Sumerian weavers' shifts than about most medieval workers.
spotlights.why_it_matters: This is one of the first large industrial workforces in history, and it made cloth.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first factory floor in history smelled of wet wool.

spotlights.name: The Kültepe textile letters
spotlights.spot_it: Small pillow-shaped clay tablets, some still in clay envelopes, written by Assyrian merchants and their wives.
spotlights.story_md: At **Kanesh** in central Anatolia, Assyrian merchants lived in a trading quarter for generations. More than **22,000** tablets have been dug up there, mostly private business letters. They trade **tin** and **textiles** brought by donkey from Ashur, about 1,000 km away, for silver. Many of the cloths were woven at home by the merchants' wives. One of them, **Taram-Kubi**, wove textiles in Ashur that were in high demand and sent them to her husband Innaya in Kanesh, who sold them and sent silver back. Her letters can be blunt about money. This is the oldest large archive of private letters, and much of it is about clothing fabric.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows women running a long-distance textile business 3,900 years ago.
spotlights.memory_hook: Taram-Kubi's looms in Ashur paid for her husband's life in Turkey.

sections.title: Egyptian men: the kilt that lasted 3,000 years
sections.intro_md:
For most of Egyptian history, a man's basic garment was the **shendyt**, a rectangle of linen wrapped around the hips and tucked or belted at the waist, usually ending above the knee. Labourers wore a short, plain one or a loincloth. Officials wore longer, finer ones. Kings wore one with a stiff pleated front and a decorated belt.

Fashion did move, slowly. In the Old Kingdom the kilt was short and close. In the Middle Kingdom it grew longer and men of rank added a stiff triangular apron. By the New Kingdom, after about 1550 BC, well-off men layered a sheer pleated shirt with sleeves over a pleated skirt, sometimes with a see-through overskirt on top. Herodotus, visiting much later, noticed that Egyptian men wore two garments and women one.

The three works below are among the best preserved images of Egyptian men's dress, from a king at the very start of Egyptian history to a seated clerk.

spotlights.name: Narmer Palette
spotlights.spot_it: A shield-shaped grey stone slab about 64 cm tall with cow-headed faces at the top and a king smiting an enemy.
spotlights.story_md: This ceremonial palette is one of the first documents of Egyptian kingship, and it is also a fashion plate. On one side **Narmer** wears the tall **White Crown** of Upper Egypt; on the other, the **Red Crown** of Lower Egypt. From the back of his belt hangs a **bull's tail**, a royal accessory kings wore for the next 3,000 years. Behind him walks an official whose only job is to carry the king's **sandals**. Found by James Quibell and Frederick Green at Hierakonpolis in 1897 to 1898, it was carved on a form of object used for grinding eye paint, which ties royal dress to cosmetics from the very start.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It fixes the royal costume, crowns, tail and sandals, at the birth of the Egyptian state.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first king of Egypt had a man just for his shoes.

spotlights.name: The Seated Scribe
spotlights.spot_it: A cross-legged man with a papyrus on his lap, painted red-brown skin, a short white kilt pulled taut across his knees, and startling crystal eyes.
spotlights.story_md: Auguste Mariette found this painted limestone figure at Saqqara on 19 November 1850. The man wears nothing but a **white kilt** stretched tight between his folded knees to make a writing desk. His eyes are inlaid with veined white magnesite and **polished rock crystal**, held in place by copper clips. His slightly soft chest and belly were a deliberate sign of status: a desk worker who did not need to labour in the fields. The kilt is plain because plain white linen was itself the luxury, and the finer and whiter it was, the higher the wearer stood.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how simple everyday elite dress was in the Old Kingdom.
spotlights.memory_hook: His kilt was his desk.

spotlights.name: The shendyt kilt
spotlights.spot_it: A wrapped linen kilt to the knee, often with a fan of pleats on one front edge and a belt at the waist.
spotlights.story_md: The shendyt was worn by everyone from farmhands to gods. It was just a wrapped cloth, but its details carried rank. Workers' kilts were short and coarse so legs could move. Officials' kilts were longer and finer. The royal shendyt had **pleats** pressed into one side, a stiffened front panel and a belt, sometimes with the bull's tail at the back. Soldiers wore versions too, because a kilt lets a man run. Pleats were made by folding damp linen and pressing it, possibly over grooved boards, and starching it with gum. They fell out each wash, which is why only people with servants could keep them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Egypt's most common garment shows how small details marked class.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Egypt, your pleats were your pay grade.

compare.difference: Both are unstitched cloths wrapped round the hips. The dhoti passes between the legs and is usually cotton; the shendyt wraps like a skirt and was linen.

sections.title: Egyptian women: the dress in the painting and the dress in the box
sections.intro_md:
Look at Egyptian art and women wear one thing for a thousand years: a **sheath dress**, tight from ankle to just under the breasts, held up by one or two shoulder straps. Statues show it covering the breasts; flat paintings, which show bodies in profile, sometimes leave one breast exposed.

Now look at the real dresses that survive in tombs. They are different. Most are **tube-shaped, sewn up one side, with sleeves**, and they are baggy. The clinging sheath was an artistic convention, a way of showing an ideal body, much as fashion illustrators today stretch legs. Egyptologists now read Egyptian art as a picture of how people wanted to be seen, not a photograph.

Wealth showed in fineness: by the New Kingdom, rich women wore linen so thin you can see the body through it in paintings, wrapped and pleated over a dress, with a shawl that could be **13 to 14 feet** long. And for one short period, some women wore dresses made of beads.

spotlights.name: Rahotep and Nofret
spotlights.spot_it: A seated couple in painted limestone: he dark-skinned with a moustache and white kilt, she pale in a white mantle, heavy black wig and flowered headband.
spotlights.story_md: Found at **Meidum** in 1871, these two statues still have most of their original paint. **Nofret** wears a close white mantle over her shoulders, a broad collar, and a thick dark **wig** cut straight; you can see her natural hairline under the edge of it. A diadem of flowers circles her head, similar to gold inlaid diadems excavated at Giza. **Rahotep**, a prince and priest, wears a short white kilt and a thin moustache. The skin colours follow a rule of Egyptian art: men painted red-brown from working outdoors, women paler from life indoors. The eyes are inlaid and look uncannily alive.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The pair is the clearest colour picture of elite dress at the time of the great pyramids.
spotlights.memory_hook: Look under Nofret's wig: her real hair is showing.

spotlights.name: The sheath dress: art versus wardrobe
spotlights.spot_it: In paintings: an ankle-length tube clinging to the body with straps over the shoulders. In museum cases: loose linen tunics with sleeves.
spotlights.story_md: The tight sheath is everywhere in Egyptian art, and yet no tight sheath survives. Real women's dresses from tombs are loose, often with sleeves, sometimes pleated, and show signs of wear and mending. Two things explain the gap. Egyptian artists drew an ideal, and an ideal body was slim, young and smooth, so the dress was drawn to show it. And statues were for eternity, so they showed the person at their perfect best. It is a useful lesson for reading any old picture: dress in art is a statement, not a record. The word 'kalasiris', still used in many books for this dress, comes from Herodotus and may not be Egyptian at all.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It teaches us to check images against surviving objects.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egyptian painters drew the dress you wished you had.

spotlights.name: The bead-net dress
spotlights.spot_it: A diamond-mesh net of blue and blue-green faience beads worn over a linen dress, with a fringe of beads at the hem.
spotlights.story_md: A handful of Old Kingdom women were buried wearing dresses made of **thousands of faience beads** strung into a net. The best known were found in a **5th Dynasty** burial at **Qau** and in a tomb at **Giza**; both had collapsed into piles of loose beads and had to be restrung from the patterns found in the grave. Paintings show goddesses and dancing girls in similar mesh. Beaded nets rattled when the wearer moved, and some scholars think they were dance costumes or garments with a ritual meaning linked to the goddess Hathor. One example had **breast caps** of beadwork.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the most striking garments to survive from the age of the pyramids.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dress that rattled when she danced.

spotlights.name: Nefertari's tomb paintings
spotlights.spot_it: A queen in a white, see-through pleated robe tied under the breast, a vulture headdress with two tall plumes, and a wide jewelled collar.
spotlights.story_md: Queen **Nefertari**, chief wife of Ramesses II, has one of the best-painted tombs in Egypt. Her clothes show the height of New Kingdom fashion. Over a dress she wears a **sheer pleated linen robe**, knotted beneath the breast, with sleeves that fall in fine folds. You can see the outline of her body through it, which was the point: only the very best linen was that thin. Her head carries a gold **vulture cap**, a sign of a queen and of the goddess Nekhbet, topped with two tall feathers. A broad collar and armlets add colour that the white linen lacks.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best surviving colour view of royal women's dress at Egypt's imperial peak.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nefertari wore linen so fine it was barely there.

sections.title: Hair: shaved heads, wigs and perfume cones
sections.intro_md:
Many Egyptian men and women of rank **shaved their heads** or cropped their hair very short, then wore **wigs** when they went out. It kept them cool and free of lice, and it let fashion change without waiting for hair to grow. Wigs were made of human hair, sometimes padded with date palm fibre, and set with beeswax and resin so curls and braids held their shape for years.

Children were different. Boys and girls had most of their head shaved but kept one long lock on the right side, the **sidelock of youth**. And at parties, in paintings from the reign of Hatshepsut onward, guests wear strange white cones on top of their wigs. For a century scholars argued whether those cones were real or just a painter's symbol. In 2019 archaeologists reported finding real ones.

Mesopotamia went the other way. Men there wore their own hair long and grew long beards, curled and oiled, while Sumerian priests shaved.

spotlights.name: Egyptian wigs
spotlights.spot_it: A heavy mass of tiny braids or tight curls, often dark brown or black, sitting on the head like a helmet and falling to the shoulders.
spotlights.story_md: Egyptian wigs were built on a net of plaited strands, with hundreds of small locks attached and set with a mix of **beeswax and resin**. Some used human hair alone; cheaper ones were bulked out with date palm fibre. Wigs grew larger and more layered over time. By the New Kingdom, a party wig might be a double wig, with curls above and long ringlets below. Owners kept them in wooden boxes, and some were buried with them. Wearing a wig over a shaved head kept the scalp cool under the sun and removed the risk of lice, a problem in any crowded ancient town.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Wigs show that Egyptian appearance was designed and changed at will.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egyptians shaved their heads so they could choose their hair each morning.

spotlights.name: The perfume head cone
spotlights.when: Depicted from c. 1470 BC; real ones found in burials, reported 2019
spotlights.spot_it: A white or yellowish cone perched on top of a wig at a banquet, often with streaks running down the hair.
spotlights.story_md: For a long time, head cones were thought to be lumps of scented fat that melted in the heat and perfumed the wig. Others thought they were just a sign in art meaning 'this person smells good' or 'this person is blessed'. No one had found one. Then a team excavating the ordinary cemetery at **Amarna**, the city of Akhenaten, found two hollow cones of a waxy material on the heads of people in simple graves, published in 2019. That proves cones were real objects, and that not only the elite wore them. Their exact purpose, perfume or ritual, is still debated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A century-old debate was settled by digging the graves of ordinary people.
spotlights.memory_hook: The party hat of ancient Egypt turned out to be real.

spotlights.name: The sidelock of youth
spotlights.spot_it: A child, or a priest playing a youthful role, with a shaved head except for one thick lock or braid curling down by the right ear.
spotlights.story_md: Egyptian children usually wore **no clothes at all** until about the age of six, though they did wear anklets, bracelets and amulets. Their hair was shaved except for one long lock on the right side. Art uses the lock as a symbol of childhood: the god Horus as a child wears it, and so do princes in reliefs, even as teenagers. Some adult priests wore a version of it to show a special role. Cutting the sidelock marked growing up. It is the clearest case of hair as a uniform in ancient Egypt: anyone looking at a figure knew its age group at once.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that age, not just class, was written on the body.
spotlights.memory_hook: One lock of hair meant 'I am still a child'.

sections.title: Faces and jewellery: colour against white linen
sections.intro_md:
If clothes were white, colour came from everything else. Egyptian men and women lined their eyes: black **kohl** made from the lead ore **galena** on the upper lid, green **malachite** on the lower lid in early periods. They reddened lips with ochre, dyed hands and nails with henna, and wore perfumes that were among the most expensive goods of the ancient world.

Jewellery was heavy and bright. Gold came from the Eastern Desert and Nubia. **Silver** was rarer than gold in Egypt because it had to be imported, and was valued more highly. Carnelian, amethyst and jasper came from the desert, turquoise from Sinai, **lapis lazuli** from Afghanistan, 3,000 km away. People who could not afford stone used glazed **faience** and coloured pottery beads. The broad collar, the bracelet, the earring and the amulet were worn by both sexes.

spotlights.name: Kohl
spotlights.spot_it: A small stone or glass tube with a stick applicator, holding black powder for thick lines around the eyes, in men and women alike.
spotlights.story_md: Egyptian eye paint was mostly **galena**, lead sulphide, ground and mixed with fat. Chemists who analysed the contents of ancient make-up jars found two lead compounds, **laurionite** and **phosgenite**, that do not occur naturally in the Nile valley. They appear to have been made on purpose, by wet chemistry, making Egyptian cosmetics one of the earliest known chemical industries. The Ebers Papyrus of about 1550 BC calls such eye paint protective. A 2010 study found that tiny doses of these lead salts made skin cells produce **nitric oxide**, which helps the immune system, which may explain the belief that kohl prevented eye infections.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Make-up in Egypt was medicine, chemistry and fashion in one jar.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egyptian eyeliner was a lab product with a medical claim.

compare.difference: Kajal is lamp soot mixed with oil or ghee; surma, like Egyptian kohl, is ground from galena and other minerals and can contain lead.

spotlights.name: Cosmetic palettes
spotlights.spot_it: A flat slab of dark grey stone, often shaped like a fish, turtle, bird or ram, with a worn hollow in the middle from grinding.
spotlights.story_md: Long before the pyramids, Egyptians ground green malachite and black galena on flat stone **palettes** to make eye paint. Thousands survive from predynastic graves, cut from greywacke into animal shapes: fish, birds, turtles and rams. Over time, a few palettes grew huge and were carved with scenes of hunts and battles, no longer for daily use but as temple offerings. The **Narmer Palette** is the most famous of these. So the most important document of the first Egyptian kingdom belongs to a family of make-up tools, which tells you how central the painted eye was to Egyptian identity.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They link everyday grooming to the first royal monuments.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egypt's first history book was a make-up tray.

spotlights.name: The broad collar (wesekh)
spotlights.when: Old Kingdom onward, from c. 2670 BC
spotlights.spot_it: A wide half-moon of rows of beads lying across the collarbones from shoulder to shoulder, often ending in two falcon heads.
spotlights.story_md: The Egyptian word **wesekh** means 'broad', and the collar is exactly that: rows of tube beads of faience, glass, stone or gold strung on linen thread, spreading over the chest. Gods wore them, and so did men and women from the Old Kingdom on. Tutankhamun was buried with several, including one inlaid with glass and stones now in the Grand Egyptian Museum. At banquets, guests wore lighter versions made of **real flowers, leaves and berries** sewn onto papyrus. Against white linen, a broad collar was the outfit's main colour, the way a printed scarf works on a plain shirt.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the single most recognisable Egyptian accessory.
spotlights.memory_hook: The wesekh did for linen what a necktie does for a shirt.

spotlights.name: The jewels of Princess Sithathoriunet

where.label: Lahun, Egypt; now Met Museum and Cairo

spotlights.spot_it: A gold pectoral of two falcons around a royal name, inlaid with tiny pieces of carnelian, lapis lazuli and turquoise set in gold cells.
spotlights.story_md: Robbers emptied the princess's tomb next to the pyramid of Senusret II in antiquity, but they missed a small mud-filled **niche**. When Flinders Petrie and Guy Brunton excavated it in **1914**, they found her jewel boxes: pectorals, a crown, bracelets, girdles and cosmetic jars. The pieces are made by **cloisonné**, with hundreds of cut stones fitted into tiny gold cells. They are often called among the finest jewellery ever found in an Egyptian tomb. Most of it is now in the Metropolitan Museum in New York; the crown is in Cairo. Brunton spent weeks washing out the mud to recover every bead.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the highest skill of Middle Kingdom jewellers.
spotlights.memory_hook: The thieves missed one muddy hole, and it held a princess's jewel box.

spotlights.name: The bronze mirror
spotlights.spot_it: A polished disc of bronze or copper on a handle, often shaped like a papyrus stem or the head of the goddess Hathor.
spotlights.story_md: Egyptians did their make-up in **polished metal**, not glass. A mirror was a disc of copper or bronze, polished until it reflected, set on a handle often carved as a papyrus stalk, a girl, or the face of **Hathor**, goddess of love and beauty. The round disc echoed the sun, and mirrors were placed in graves as well as used in life. Cosmetic sets buried together included a kohl tube, a razor, tweezers, a whetstone and a mirror, a toolkit you could still use today. Shaving was part of beauty for women too: body hair was widely removed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reminds us that ancient beauty was a daily routine with real tools.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egypt's mirror was a small sun on a stick.

sections.title: Feet: mostly bare
sections.intro_md:
Most Egyptians, most of the time, went **barefoot**. Sandals were for special occasions, for rough ground, for the rich and for the gods. That is why the king on the Narmer Palette needs a servant to carry his: you put them on when you arrived, not on the walk.

Sandals were made of **papyrus**, **palm leaf** or **leather**, sewn in coils or woven, with a thong between the first two toes. Herodotus says priests were only allowed papyrus ones. In royal tombs, sandals turn up in gold. Tutankhamun's body was found with gold sandals and gold stalls on every toe and finger.

Socks came much later. The famous red Egyptian 'toe socks', split between the big toe and the rest so they could be worn with sandals, date from around AD 300 to 500, three millennia after the pyramids.

spotlights.name: Tutankhamun's sandals

where.label: Valley of the Kings; now Grand Egyptian Museum

spotlights.spot_it: Flat-soled sandals of gold sheet or veneered wood with a strap between the toes, beside gold covers for each toe.
spotlights.story_md: Tutankhamun's tomb held sandals of many kinds: plain papyrus and rush ones, leather ones, sandals veneered with bark and gold, and a pair of **gold sandals** placed on his feet inside the mummy wrappings with **gold toe stalls** to keep each toe intact for eternity. One veneered pair is famous for its insoles, which show **bound foreign enemies**, so that the king trod on Egypt's foes with each step. The range, from simple everyday sandals to funerary gold, shows that the same king owned work shoes and ceremonial shoes, much like anyone today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show that even a king's wardrobe was split between daily wear and display.
spotlights.memory_hook: Tutankhamun walked on his enemies, literally.

spotlights.name: Egyptian toe socks
spotlights.spot_it: A bright red woollen sock with a split toe, like a mitten for the foot, made to wear with a thong sandal.
spotlights.story_md: These look like a modern novelty but they are about 1,600 years old, from **Oxyrhynchus** in Roman-ruled Egypt. They were not knitted. They were made by **nalbinding**, an older technique where a single needle loops short lengths of yarn into fabric. The toe is divided into two compartments, one for the big toe and one for the rest, so the sock fits under a sandal strap, the same idea as Japanese tabi. They come up here because many people picture them as 'Pharaonic' socks. They are not: they belong to a time of Christian monasteries, long after the last pharaoh.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are a clear example of how 'ancient Egypt' gets blurred across 3,000 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pharaohs never wore these; Romans and Christians in Egypt did.

sections.title: Kings and queens: crowns, beards and borrowed bodies
sections.intro_md:
Royal dress in Egypt was a uniform for a job that had to look the same for 3,000 years. A king wore a pleated kilt with a bull's tail, a broad collar, and on his head one of several crowns: the **White Crown** of the south, the **Red Crown** of the north, the two combined as the **Double Crown**, the blue **khepresh** war helmet, or the striped **nemes** headcloth. On his chin he tied a **false beard** of plaited hair. On his brow reared the **uraeus**, a cobra ready to spit fire at enemies.

One astonishing fact: not a single Egyptian crown has ever been found. We know them only from statues, paintings and texts. Some Egyptologists think crowns were kept in temples and passed from king to king, or were destroyed when dynasties fell.

Because the costume was so fixed, it could be worn by someone who did not fit the usual body. When Hatshepsut became king, she wore it too, beard and all.

spotlights.name: Tutankhamun's mask and the nemes
spotlights.spot_it: A gold face framed by a headcloth with blue and gold stripes falling in two lappets onto the chest, a cobra and vulture on the brow and a plaited beard.
spotlights.story_md: The mask weighs about **10.23 kg** and stands 54 cm tall. It shows the king wearing the **nemes**, a striped linen headcloth pulled tight over the brow and tied at the back into a tail, with two lappets hanging forward over the shoulders. The blue stripes are **glass**, not lapis. On his brow sit the cobra and vulture of the two halves of Egypt. In August 2014 the beard came off during cleaning, and staff glued it back with epoxy, leaving it crooked; a German-Egyptian team fixed it in 2015 with beeswax. The mask is now in the Grand Egyptian Museum.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous image of an Egyptian royal headdress.
spotlights.memory_hook: The blue on the world's most famous mask is glass.

spotlights.name: The Double Crown (pschent)
spotlights.when: First known on King Djet, 1st Dynasty
spotlights.spot_it: A tall white bowling-pin crown sitting inside a red crown with a flat back and a curling wire at the front.
spotlights.story_md: Egyptians called it **sekhemty**, 'the Two Powerful Ones'. It combined the **White Crown** of Upper Egypt with the **Red Crown** of Lower Egypt, so putting it on announced that the king ruled both. Tradition credited its invention to Menes, the legendary unifier; the first king known to wear it is **Djet** of the 1st Dynasty. And yet no pschent, and no Egyptian crown of any kind, has ever been found. We do not know what the White Crown was made of: felt, leather, linen over a frame, or something else. Everything we know comes from images and texts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most important object in Egyptian royal dress, and it has vanished completely.
spotlights.memory_hook: Thousands of pictures, zero crowns.

spotlights.name: Hatshepsut in the king's costume
spotlights.spot_it: A seated or kneeling figure with a woman's face but a king's nemes headcloth, kilt and tied-on false beard.
spotlights.story_md: Hatshepsut began her reign as regent for her stepson and then took the throne as king. Her early images show her as a woman in a dress. Mid-reign images mix a gown with a king's crown and beard. Later ones show her in the full male costume: **nemes or khat headcloth, uraeus, shendyt kilt and false beard**. This was not disguise. Kingship was a role with a fixed costume, and she wore the uniform of the office. After her death her images were chiselled away or smashed and buried at Deir el-Bahari, late in the reign of Thutmose III. Scholars still debate whether that was hatred or routine politics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Her statues show that royal dress described an office, not a body.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egypt's greatest female king wore a beard to work.

spotlights.name: Nefertiti's flat-topped crown
spotlights.spot_it: A woman's head on a long neck under a tall flat-topped blue crown with a gold band, a broad floral collar, and one empty eye socket.
spotlights.story_md: The bust was found in the workshop of the sculptor **Thutmose** at Amarna by a German team under Ludwig Borchardt on 6 December 1912. Nefertiti wears a crown no one else wore: a tall, **flat-topped blue cap** with a gold diadem band and a broken uraeus at the front, so her own hair is completely hidden. Below it is a broad collar of painted petals. The left eye inlay is missing, perhaps because it was a workshop model. Egypt has asked for the bust back since 1924; Germany says it was acquired legally. It is one of the most copied images of beauty in the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a royal woman could have a signature headdress of her own.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nefertiti's crown was her logo.

sections.title: Priests, workers and slaves: what rank looked like
sections.intro_md:
In Egypt the gap between rich and poor showed most clearly in linen. The rich wore fine, nearly transparent cloth, in layers. Farmers and labourers wore a short, coarse kilt or a **loincloth**, and in the heat many worked in very little. Children often wore nothing at all.

Priests followed rules of purity. Herodotus, writing around 440 BC, says they wore **only linen**, kept it constantly washed, wore sandals of papyrus, and **shaved their whole bodies every other day**. Wool, he says, was never taken into temples or buried with the dead, though archaeologists have found some woollen garments in graves, so the rule may have been stricter in some places and periods than others.

One priest stood out: the **sem**, who performed the funeral rite called the Opening of the Mouth, wore a **leopard skin** over his linen, the spotted head and paws hanging down his body.

spotlights.name: The sem priest's leopard skin
spotlights.spot_it: A shaven-headed priest wearing a whole leopard skin over white linen, the cat's head on his belly and the spotted paws dangling.
spotlights.story_md: In the tomb of Tutankhamun, the painted wall of the burial chamber shows his successor **Ay** dressed as a sem priest, in a leopard skin, performing the **Opening of the Mouth** on the dead king's mummy. Doing the rite was a way of claiming the throne. Leopard skins, some real and some imitation ones made of linen painted with spots or sewn with stars, are known from tombs. The skin came from the south, from Nubia and beyond, and so it was rare and powerful. Kings also wore leopard and lion skins as signs of status.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how one garment could mark a sacred job and even a claim to power.
spotlights.memory_hook: To bury a king and become one, you put on a leopard.

spotlights.name: The leather net loincloth
spotlights.spot_it: A gazelle-skin loincloth cut into a fine diamond net with a solid patch at the seat, so it looks like lace made of leather.
spotlights.story_md: Workmen, soldiers and sailors sometimes wore a loincloth of **gazelle leather** slit all over with thousands of tiny cuts, so that it stretched into a net. It was cool, did not trap sweat, and lasted longer than linen, with a solid patch where it would wear out from sitting on rowing benches. A few survive in museums, including a fine example in Boston. Rich men wore linen loincloths under their kilts too; Tutankhamun's tomb held a large number of triangular linen loincloths. The net leather version is one of the cleverest pieces of working clothing to survive from the ancient world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the practical engineering in clothes meant for physical labour.
spotlights.memory_hook: Egyptian rowers wore leather lace.

sections.title: Tutankhamun's wardrobe: the closet that broke the stereotype
sections.intro_md:
When Howard Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb in November 1922 he found **5,398 objects**. Among them were boxes of clothes: tunics, shirts, kilts, shawls, sashes, loincloths, headcloths, **gloves**, and dozens of sandals. Many textiles had rotted to black powder and most leather had melted into a pitch-like mass. But what survived changed how scholars think about Egyptian dress.

The clothes were not all white. Tunics were decorated with **woven bands, embroidery and beadwork** in red, blue, yellow and green. There were loose, comfortable tunics that look like nothing in the official art of his time. There were child-sized garments, perhaps clothes the king wore as a boy. And there was a painted wooden **mannequin** of his head and torso, which Carter thought may have been used to fit or display his clothes.

The lesson: Egyptian art showed an ideal and a uniform. The real royal wardrobe was more colourful, more practical and more personal.

spotlights.name: Tutankhamun's tunics and gloves

where.label: Valley of the Kings; now Grand Egyptian Museum

spotlights.spot_it: Loose linen tunics with coloured woven borders and embroidered panels, and linen gloves cut like modern ones with separate fingers.
spotlights.story_md: The king's tunics are the opposite of the stiff white kilt. Some are **decorated with tapestry bands** and embroidery showing animals and plants in colour, a technique Egypt may have learned from western Asia. There are linen **gloves**, some embroidered, found in the antechamber and annexe; gloves are almost never shown in Egyptian art, yet the king owned several pairs. Some textile historians think they were for driving a chariot. Many garments were folded and packed in chests, as if for a journey. Study of the clothing by textile specialists in the 1990s confirmed that most were real, worn garments, not just tomb props.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They prove Egyptian royal dress was far more colourful than the official art suggests.
spotlights.memory_hook: The boy king packed embroidered shirts and driving gloves for eternity.

spotlights.name: The mannequin of Tutankhamun
spotlights.spot_it: A life-size painted wooden head and chest of the king with no arms, wearing a flat-topped yellow crown and a painted white shirt.
spotlights.story_md: In the antechamber Carter found a **wooden torso** of the king, painted with a white garment and topped by a crown with a cobra. It has no arms or legs. Carter suggested it was a **dressmaker's dummy**, used to try on or show the king's clothes and jewellery, which would make it the oldest known mannequin. Other scholars think it had a ritual purpose, perhaps as a stand-in for the king's body. Either way, it is the right size for the king and has the same face as his other images. Its purpose is still uncertain.
spotlights.why_it_matters: If Carter was right, fashion's oldest tool is 3,300 years old.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first fashion dummy may have belonged to a teenage king.

sections.title: Sumer: dressed in sheep
sections.intro_md:
Across the desert, the first cities of southern Iraq, **Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish**, grew rich on barley and sheep. The earliest Sumerian clothing we can see, on carvings from around 3200 BC, is a simple kilt or a close-fitting net skirt for the lower body. Priests in the earliest scenes go **naked**, which in Sumer was a sign of purity before the gods.

Then came the **kaunakes**, the Greek name for the most recognisable garment of Sumer. At first it was a sheepskin worn with the fleece outside. Around 2500 BC, woven wool with long tufts or loops replaced the real skin, so the skirt looked like overlapping petals or locks of fleece. Short versions marked soldiers and servants; long ones reaching the ankle marked rulers and priests. Women wore similar tufted cloth as a robe over one shoulder, leaving the **right shoulder and arm bare**.

The statues of Sumer are small, stiff and wide-eyed, made to stand in temples and pray forever on their owners' behalf. Their clothes tell us who they were.

rows.Egypt: Usually bare, or a sheer shirt later
rows.Sumer: Bare, or a shawl over one shoulder

spotlights.name: The Warka Vase
spotlights.spot_it: A slim alabaster vase about a metre tall carved in bands: sheep at the bottom, naked men carrying baskets in the middle, a goddess and a figure in a long belted garment at the top.
spotlights.story_md: This vase from **Uruk** is one of the oldest narrative carvings in the world. In the bottom band, rams and ewes walk in a line, the wealth of Sumer. In the middle, a file of **naked men** carry offerings of food. At the top, a ruler-figure in a ceremonial kilt with a **long belt** brings gifts to a female deity at her shrine. Clothing marks rank: the most important man is the only one dressed. In April 2003 the vase was ripped from its case during the looting of the Iraq Museum. It was **returned on 12 June 2003**, broken into 14 pieces, and has since been restored.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows dress and nakedness used as signs of status at the birth of cities.
spotlights.memory_hook: On the oldest story vase, only the boss wears clothes.

spotlights.name: Ebih-Il of Mari
spotlights.spot_it: A small seated alabaster man with a shaved head, long beard, hands clasped, enormous blue eyes and a fluffy skirt of long tufts.
spotlights.story_md: André Parrot found this statue in the Temple of Ishtar at **Mari** in January 1934: the head one day, the body the next. **Ebih-Il** was an official, a superintendent, and the statue was his stand-in, praying to Ishtar forever. His eyes are shell with **lapis lazuli** irises. The famous detail is his skirt: a **kaunakes**, carved in long wavy locks that look like real sheepskin, possibly goatskin. The back of the skirt even shows a tail-like tuft. At only 52.5 cm tall, it is one of the best preserved Sumerian-style statues anywhere.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the textbook image of the kaunakes skirt.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ebih-Il went to temple in a sheepskin skirt and has been praying since 2400 BC.

spotlights.name: The Tell Asmar worshippers
spotlights.spot_it: A group of stiff standing figures with clasped hands, huge black-ringed eyes, long beards, and simple skirts with a patterned hem.
spotlights.story_md: Twelve statues were found buried together under the floor of a temple of the god **Abu** at Eshnunna: ten men and two women. Their eyes are shell and black limestone, with lapis pupils on one. The men wear plain **wrapped skirts** that cover the waist and thighs, ending in a decorated hem, with long hair and beards; the women wear robes over one shoulder. They were placed in the temple to stand in permanent prayer for the people who paid for them. Today they are split between Baghdad, New York and Chicago.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They show ordinary Sumerian worshippers' clothes rather than kings'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wide eyes, clasped hands, Sunday best, for 4,500 years.

spotlights.name: The Standard of Ur

where.label: Royal Cemetery of Ur; now British Museum

spotlights.spot_it: A small box with two long sides of shell figures on bright blue lapis lazuli: chariots and soldiers on one, a banquet and animals on the other.
spotlights.story_md: Leonard Woolley found this box in tomb PG 779 at Ur. Its purpose is unknown; Woolley's guess of a 'standard' carried on a pole is now doubted. It is a catalogue of Sumerian dress in about 49 by 22 cm. On the **Peace** side, men in **fringed skirts** bring animals and goods to a banquet where the king, larger than the rest, wears a long tufted skirt. On the **War** side, soldiers wear helmets and **leather cloaks** with spots, perhaps studded for protection, and helmets like those found in the same tomb. The materials, lapis from Afghanistan and red limestone, show Ur's long trade reach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Sumerian dress for peace and war side by side.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two sides of Sumer: banquet skirts and battle cloaks.

spotlights.name: Puabi and her headdress
spotlights.spot_it: A huge headdress of gold leaves, gold ribbons and gold flowers on a wig, with lapis and carnelian beads falling across the chest.
spotlights.story_md: Woolley found **Puabi**'s tomb almost intact. Her cylinder seal names her 'Queen Puabi' with no mention of a husband, which suggests she held power in her own right. She died at about 40 and was buried with **52 attendants**, many of them women wearing gold headdresses of their own. Her headdress has rows of gold ribbons, wreaths of gold leaves and gold flowers, and huge gold earrings; strings of **lapis** from Afghanistan and **carnelian**, some of it probably from the Indus, covered her upper body. Her body is in London's Natural History Museum; her jewels are in Philadelphia, London and Baghdad.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the richest surviving outfit from the ancient Near East.
spotlights.memory_hook: Puabi went to her grave in a garden of gold.

sections.title: Akkad, Babylon and Assyria: fringes, shawls and beards
sections.intro_md:
After about 2300 BC Mesopotamian dress changed. The tufted kaunakes gave way to woven wool cloths, often very long, wrapped around the body and over **one shoulder** like a giant shawl, with **fringes** along the edges. A ruler like **Gudea** of Lagash, around 2140 BC, wears a plain robe draped over the left shoulder with the right arm free, and a round brimmed cap.

Gods kept the old tufted, flounced robes and wore **horned crowns**, the sign of divinity. When the Akkadian king Naram-Sin put horns on his own helmet, he was claiming to be a god.

By the time of the **Neo-Assyrian** empire, from about 900 BC, royal dress had become heavy and dazzling: ankle-length tunics, fringed shawls wrapped in a spiral, rich embroidery, armbands, earrings and bracelets, and beards and hair in rows of tight, oiled curls. Herodotus, describing the Babylonians in the 5th century BC, says they wore a **linen tunic to the feet, a wool tunic over it, and a short white cloak**, grew their hair long, wore turbans, perfumed their whole bodies, and every man carried a **seal and a carved walking stick**.

spotlights.name: Victory Stele of Naram-Sin

where.label: Sippar, then Susa; now the Louvre

spotlights.spot_it: A tall pinkish stone slab with a king climbing a mountain over fallen enemies, wearing a helmet with horns, under stars at the summit.
spotlights.story_md: The Akkadian king **Naram-Sin** had himself carved trampling the Lullubi, a mountain people of the Zagros. He is larger than everyone else, and his helmet has **horns**, at that time worn only by gods. The horns were a fashion statement with a theological message: the king was claiming divine status. Around the 12th century BC the Elamite king **Shutruk-Nakhunte** carried the stele off as loot from Sippar to Susa and added his own inscription. Jacques de Morgan excavated it there in 1898. It is now in the Louvre, about 2 metres tall.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a piece of headgear used to claim godhood.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two horns on a helmet made a king a god.

spotlights.name: Gudea of Lagash
spotlights.spot_it: A calm seated or standing man in polished black diorite, hands clasped, wearing a plain robe over the left shoulder and a round cap with a thick brim.
spotlights.story_md: **Gudea** ruled the city-state of Lagash for about twenty years and filled its temples with statues of himself, carved in hard **diorite** shipped from Magan, modern Oman. He is shown in a long, plain **robe wrapped over his left shoulder**, leaving the right arm bare, with a fringed edge; on his head is a round cap with a thick, textured brim, perhaps fur or wool. The style is modest compared with earlier tufted skirts, matching his chosen title, *ensi*, governor, rather than king. His inscriptions name traders from **Meluhha**, probably the Indus, bringing gold dust and carnelian.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Gudea's statues fix the look of a pious Sumerian ruler.
spotlights.memory_hook: Gudea dressed like a humble governor in the hardest stone money could buy.

spotlights.name: The top of Hammurabi's law stele
spotlights.spot_it: A 2.25 m black stone pillar; at the top a standing man in a cap and long robe faces a seated god in a tiered robe and horned crown with rays at his shoulders.
spotlights.story_md: The top of the stele shows **Hammurabi** of Babylon before **Shamash**, god of the sun and justice. The god wears a **horned crown** and a long robe of rows of flounces, the old divine dress; flames rise from his shoulders. Hammurabi wears a round cap with a brim and a long robe draped over one shoulder, his right arm raised in respect. The scene says: these laws come from the god. Below, about 4,130 lines of text set out the laws, up to law 282. The stele was found at Susa in 1901 to 1902, taken there as loot centuries after it was carved.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the costume difference between a god and a king in one frame.
spotlights.memory_hook: The god wore ruffles; the king wore a cap.

spotlights.name: Ashurnasirpal II's palace reliefs
spotlights.spot_it: Giant gypsum wall panels of bearded men in long fringed robes, every surface of the cloth carved with tiny patterns, with curled hair and beards in rows.
spotlights.story_md: **Ashurnasirpal II** lined his new palace at Kalhu (Nimrud) with carved stone panels showing himself, his courtiers and winged spirits. The carvers recorded dress in fine detail: ankle-length tunics with short sleeves, a **fringed shawl** wound around the body, tassels, armbands, bracelets, earrings and daggers in the belt. The king's robe is covered in **embroidered** scenes, tiny pictures of the same kind of hunts and rituals that the reliefs show, so the clothing repeats the palace's message. He opened the palace with a ten-day feast for **69,574** guests. The reliefs are now spread across museums from London to New York.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the best record of the most elaborate royal dress of the Iron Age.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ashurnasirpal wore pictures of his own power stitched onto his robe.

spotlights.name: Lamassu: beards in stone

where.label: Khorsabad and Nimrud; Louvre, British Museum, Met

spotlights.spot_it: A colossal winged bull with a bearded human head, a horned cap, and, if you look from an angle, five legs.
spotlights.story_md: These guardians stood at palace doorways. Their faces show the Assyrian ideal of male grooming: a long rectangular **beard in rows of tight curls**, hair curled at the nape, and a **horned cap** to show divine power. The carvers gave them **five legs**, so that from the front they stand still and from the side they walk. Assyrian kings and courtiers are shown with the same beards, which were probably oiled, curled with hot tongs and partly lengthened with false hair. Several were smashed by the Islamic State group at Nineveh and Nimrud in 2015.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They set the image of the Assyrian man: bearded, curled and imposing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Assyrian beards were so important that the guard bulls had them too.

spotlights.name: The Nimrud queens' tombs
spotlights.spot_it: Gold crowns of winged figures and grapevines, heavy gold anklets, bracelets and earrings, laid out in cases in Baghdad.
spotlights.story_md: In 1988 Iraqi archaeologists found **four tombs of Assyrian queens** under the palace floors at Nimrud. Assyrian kings were buried at Ashur, but their queens lay at Kalhu. The tombs held one of the greatest gold finds of the 20th century: crowns, earrings, armlets, anklets and hundreds of small gold appliqués once sewn onto clothes so that robes **glittered**. They give the clearest idea of how much metal Assyrian royal women wore. The treasure was hidden in a bank vault during the wars of 1991 and 2003 and survived; much of the site itself was bulldozed by the Islamic State group in 2015.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proves Assyrian queens' dress was heavy with gold, sewn right onto the cloth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Assyrian queens wore robes that clinked.

spotlights.name: Herodotus describes the Babylonians
spotlights.spot_it: A Greek traveller's checklist: a linen tunic to the feet, a wool tunic over it, a short white cloak, long hair, turbans, perfume, a seal and a carved stick.
spotlights.story_md: The Greek historian **Herodotus** described Babylonian dress in Book 1 of his *Histories*. Men wore a **linen tunic** reaching the feet, a **wool tunic** over it, and a little white cloak on top, with shoes of a local style. They grew their hair long, wore turbans and perfumed the whole body. Every man carried a **seal** and a walking stick topped with a carved **apple, rose, lily or eagle**, because a plain stick was not done. Herodotus was writing about the Persian-ruled city of his own day, and he was not always reliable, but this matches the seals and fringed robes known from Babylonian art.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the only eyewitness-style description of Mesopotamian dress from the ancient world.
spotlights.memory_hook: In Babylon you were not dressed without a seal and a fancy stick.

sections.title: Dress and the law: the first veil rule
sections.intro_md:
Clothing has always been a way to sort people, and in Assyria the state wrote the sorting into law. The **Middle Assyrian Laws**, a set of tablets drawn up between about 1450 and 1250 BC and copied under Tiglath-Pileser I (reigned 1114 to 1076 BC), include the **earliest known law about veiling**.

The point of the law was not modesty in general. It was a **badge of rank**. Wives, widows and daughters of free men had to cover their heads in the street. Prostitutes and slave women were **forbidden** to veil, so that everyone could tell at a glance which women belonged to a household and which did not. Breaking the rule, or failing to report someone who did, brought public, physical punishment.

The law is a reminder that a garment's meaning is set by a society, and it can change completely over 3,000 years: the same piece of cloth has meant status, piety, protest and fashion in different places and times.

spotlights.name: The Middle Assyrian veil law
spotlights.when: Laws c. 1450 to 1250 BC; tablet copied c. 1100 BC
spotlights.spot_it: A large clay tablet densely written in cuneiform, found at Ashur, now in Berlin's Vorderasiatisches Museum.
spotlights.story_md: The law says married women, widows and Assyrian women going into the street must have their heads covered. A **prostitute** must not veil. If a man sees a veiled prostitute, he must seize her and bring her to the palace entrance, where she gets **50 blows with rods** and has **hot pitch poured on her head**. A **slave woman** caught veiled has her **ears cut off**. And a man who sees such a woman and lets her go is himself beaten 50 times, and the person who informs on him may take his clothes. The tablets were found by German excavators at Ashur in the early 20th century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the oldest written law about who may and may not cover their head.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first veil law was about who was forbidden to wear one.

sections.title: The India connection: cotton, carnelian and kajal
sections.intro_md:
The Indus valley was the third great river civilisation of the Bronze Age, and it traded with Mesopotamia directly. Sumerian texts call a land to the east **Meluhha**, which most scholars identify with the Indus, and say its ships brought carnelian, gold dust and other goods. Indus etched carnelian beads turn up in the Royal Cemetery of Ur.

The Indus also gave the world **cotton**. The oldest cotton thread known was found at **Mehrgarh** in Balochistan, preserved inside a string of copper beads, from the 6th millennium BC. By the 3rd millennium BC there were cotton cloths and spindle whorls at **Mohenjo-daro**. Egypt and Mesopotamia did not weave much cotton in this period, but Greeks and Assyrians had heard of it: Herodotus marvelled at Indian trees that grew 'wool', and Assyria's King Sennacherib may have imported cotton plants for his gardens at Nineveh.

And look at a Rajasthani woman's eyes or a man in a dhoti and you can see living relatives of ancient ideas.

spotlights.name: The world's oldest cotton
spotlights.spot_it: A white, fluffy cotton boll bursting from its dried brown case on a shrub, the source of the fibre.
spotlights.story_md: In a grave at **Mehrgarh**, archaeologists found eight copper beads strung on a thread. The copper had slowly mineralised the thread, preserving it, and microscope study showed it was **cotton**, from the 6th millennium BC, the oldest known in the world. By the 3rd millennium BC, **Mohenjo-daro** had cotton textiles and spindle whorls. Cotton later became India's great export: Herodotus, writing in the 5th century BC, described Indian trees whose 'wool' was better than sheep's. For thousands of years after that, Indian cotton cloth dressed much of the world.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes South Asia the first home of the fibre most people wear today.
spotlights.memory_hook: The oldest cotton survived because copper beads pickled it.

spotlights.name: The Priest-King's trefoil cloak

where.label: Mohenjo-daro; now National Museum of Pakistan, Karachi

spotlights.spot_it: A small bearded man in soapstone, eyes half closed, a band across his forehead, and a cloak over one shoulder covered in three-lobed trefoil shapes.
spotlights.story_md: Found at **Mohenjo-daro** in the 1920s, this 17.5 cm figure is the best image of dress in the Indus civilisation. He wears a **cloak over the left shoulder**, leaving the right shoulder bare, the same arrangement seen on Mesopotamian statues. The cloak is covered in **trefoils** and circles that still hold traces of **red** paste, perhaps imitating a printed or appliquéd cloth. Trefoil patterns also appear in Mesopotamia and Egypt. The name 'Priest-King' was given by Mortimer Wheeler and is pure guesswork. Whether the shared style means direct influence is debated.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the Indus civilisation's clearest picture of a garment.
spotlights.memory_hook: Right shoulder bare, from Ur to Mohenjo-daro.

spotlights.name: Indus etched carnelian beads at Ur
spotlights.spot_it: Orange-red stone beads with crisp white lines or circles drawn on the surface, strung with gold and blue lapis.
spotlights.story_md: Indus craftsmen invented a way to decorate carnelian: paint a design on the bead with a paste of **washing soda and plant juice**, then fire it, and the design turns permanently **white**. Beads made this way were found in the **Royal Cemetery of Ur**, from about 2600 to 2450 BC, in necklaces with gold and lapis. Others turned up at Kish, Nippur and Susa; one at Susa even bears a dedication by the Ur king **Shulgi**. Gudea's inscriptions mention carnelian from **Meluhha**. So a Sumerian noblewoman's jewellery could carry Indian craftsmanship, 2,500 km from where it was made.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are physical proof of trade in fashion goods between the Indus and Sumer.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sumer's queens wore Indian beads.

spotlights.name: Kajal and surma
spotlights.spot_it: A dark line of kajal along the eyes of a bride or a baby, or a small silver surmedani holding grey surma powder.
spotlights.story_md: Lining the eyes with black is one of the longest-lived beauty habits on earth. **Kajal** in India is traditionally made by burning oil or ghee under a lid and mixing the soot with oil; it is put on babies and brides to ward off the evil eye. **Surma**, used across North India, Pakistan and the Middle East, is ground from minerals, often **galena**, the same lead ore as ancient Egyptian kohl. Ayurvedic texts describe medicated eye salves, **anjana**. Both kajal and surma have been linked to lead poisoning, which is the dark side of a 5,000-year-old idea.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a direct living descendant of the painted eye of Egypt and Sumer.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your grandmother's kajal and Nefertiti's kohl are cousins.

spotlights.name: Dhoti and shendyt: unstitched wisdom
spotlights.spot_it: A single rectangle of cloth wrapped around the hips and tucked at the waist, with no seams at all.
spotlights.story_md: The Egyptian **shendyt** and the Indian **dhoti** are not related by descent, but they solve the same problem the same way: a hot climate, a loom that makes rectangles, and no need to cut. An unstitched cloth wastes nothing, can be retied tighter or looser, washes easily and suits any body. That is why wrapped garments dominated the ancient world from the Nile to the Ganges, and why the dhoti, lungi, mundu and sari are still worn by hundreds of millions. Cut-and-sewn trousers spread mainly with horse-riding peoples, who needed them in the saddle.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that the ancient logic of wrapped cloth is alive in India today.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same rectangle, same sun, two rivers apart.

sections.title: Myths and misreadings
sections.intro_md:
Our picture of ancient dress comes mostly from three places: tomb art, Hollywood and the 1920s. All three distort it.

**Myth: Egyptians wore only white.** Mostly natural linen, yes, but Tutankhamun's tunics had coloured woven bands and embroidery, and bead dresses and collars added colour.

**Myth: the clinging sheath dress was everyday wear.** Surviving dresses are loose tubes with sleeves. The sheath is an artistic ideal.

**Myth: Egyptians never wore wool.** Herodotus says wool was kept out of temples and graves, but woollen cloth existed and was used.

**Myth: 'kalasiris' is the Egyptian word for a dress.** The term comes from Herodotus and is used loosely by modern writers.

**Myth: the Egyptian toe socks are pharaonic.** They date to around AD 300 to 500.

**Myth: Cleopatra looked like Elizabeth Taylor.** Cleopatra VII was a Greek-speaking Ptolemaic queen who ruled 1,300 years after Tutankhamun; her coins and portraits show a Greek hairstyle and diadem. The 1963 film won an Oscar for costume design, not for accuracy.

spotlights.name: The real Cleopatra's look
spotlights.spot_it: A marble head of a woman with her hair in a 'melon' style, ridged sections pulled back to a bun, and a flat royal diadem band.
spotlights.story_md: Cleopatra VII lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid. She was a member of the **Ptolemaic dynasty**, Macedonian Greeks who had ruled Egypt since Alexander. Her Roman-era marble portraits and her coins show a Greek hairstyle, the **melon coiffure**, and a simple ribbon **diadem**, the sign of a Hellenistic monarch. In Egyptian temples she was carved in traditional pharaonic dress, but that was official art. The kohl-heavy eyes, beaded wigs and gold collars of the 1963 film come from Egyptian art 1,000 years older, filtered through Hollywood.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how films blend 3,000 years of Egypt into one costume.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cleopatra wore a Greek hairdo, not a Hollywood wig.

spotlights.name: The 'kalasiris' problem
spotlights.spot_it: A word in almost every fashion history book, used for a long Egyptian dress, that no Egyptian is known to have used.
spotlights.story_md: Many costume books call the long Egyptian dress or robe a **kalasiris**. The word comes from **Herodotus**, who used it for a fringed linen garment of the Egyptians, and also for a group of Egyptian soldiers. Egyptian texts have their own words for garments, and they do not neatly match the categories that costume books built in the 19th and 20th centuries. Modern textile specialists prefer descriptive terms: sheath dress, bag tunic, wrap-around dress, kilt. The lesson is general: when a garment name is Greek, it is a foreigner's label, not the wearer's own.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It warns that fashion history's vocabulary can come from outsiders.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kalasiris is what a Greek tourist called it.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
Ancient dress is not a closed subject. New finds and new museums keep changing what we can see.

- **1 November 2025:** the **Grand Egyptian Museum** at Giza officially opened, at a cost of about **$1.2 billion**. For the first time all **5,398** objects from Tutankhamun's tomb are shown together, in two halls, including his clothes, gloves, sandals and jewellery. About 18,000 visitors came on the first day after the opening.
- **18 September 2025:** Egypt's Interior Ministry said a 3,000-year-old **gold bracelet of King Amenemope** had been stolen from a Cairo museum, sold and melted down, and that suspects had been arrested. It is a sharp reminder that ancient jewellery is still at risk.
- **19 February 2025:** the tomb of **Thutmose II**, Hatshepsut's husband, was announced, the first royal tomb found since Tutankhamun's in 1922.
- **February 2026:** archaeologists reported a 5,300-year-old copper-alloy drill from Predynastic Egypt, the age of the Tarkhan dress.
- **July and September 2026:** France and the United States returned looted artefacts to Syria, part of a slow return of Mesopotamian heritage.

spotlights.name: The Grand Egyptian Museum
spotlights.spot_it: A vast wedge-shaped building of translucent stone panels on the desert edge, with the Giza pyramids on the skyline.
spotlights.story_md: The museum took more than two decades and about **$1.2 billion** to build. It holds over 100,000 artefacts, with more than 20,000 shown for the first time. The headline is the complete **Tutankhamun** collection, all 5,398 pieces, displayed together for the first time since Carter's day. For anyone interested in ancient dress, this means the king's tunics, gloves, sandals, collars and the gold mask can be seen in one place. Tutankhamun's mummy stays in his tomb in the Valley of the Kings. The opening was delayed several times, the last by the Iran-Israel war of June 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is now the single best place on earth to see real ancient Egyptian clothing.
spotlights.memory_hook: The boy king's whole closet finally hangs in one room.

spotlights.name: The melted bracelet of Amenemope
spotlights.spot_it: A gold bangle with beads of lapis lazuli from the burial of a 21st Dynasty king, now lost for good.
spotlights.story_md: King **Amenemope** ruled around 1000 BC from Tanis in the Nile Delta, and his burial produced gold jewellery including this bracelet. In September 2025 Egypt's Interior Ministry said it had been **stolen from a museum laboratory in Cairo**, sold through a chain of dealers and **melted down** with other gold. Suspects were arrested. The case caused alarm because the bracelet was meant to travel for an exhibition. It shows the weakness of the material record: gold jewellery survives 3,000 years in a tomb and can disappear in days for its weight in metal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reminds us that ancient adornment survives only if it is guarded.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three thousand years in a tomb, three days to a melting pot.

sections.title: How we know, and what to remember
sections.intro_md:
Everything you read today rests on four kinds of evidence, each with its own bias.

- **Surviving cloth.** Egypt's dry sand preserved real garments, from the Tarkhan dress to Tutankhamun's tunics. Mesopotamia's wetter soil destroyed almost all its textiles, so its cloth is known mostly secondhand.
- **Art.** Statues, reliefs and paintings show what people wanted to look like, not what they wore every day. Egyptian art idealises; Assyrian art shows kings at their most powerful.
- **Texts.** Ur III ration lists, Kültepe letters, laws, inventories and laundry lists show the business side of clothing. Greek writers like Herodotus add an outsider's view, useful but not always reliable.
- **Science.** Radiocarbon dates garments, chemistry identifies make-up, microscopes find cotton in copper beads.

**Remember these:** Egypt in linen, Mesopotamia in wool. The oldest garment is the Tarkhan dress. The shendyt kilt for men, the sheath dress in art but loose tunics in life. Wigs over shaved heads, head cones were real, kohl was chemistry. No Egyptian crown survives. The kaunakes was sheep turned into a skirt. Assyria wrote the first veil law. And the Indus gave the world cotton and traded beads to Ur.

best_facts.fact: The oldest woven garment known, the Tarkhan dress, spent 65 years filed with 'funerary rags' before conservators noticed it in 1977.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 5,000-year-old shirt was nearly thrown out.

best_facts.fact: Not a single ancient Egyptian crown has ever been found. Every crown we know is from statues, paintings and texts.
best_facts.why_surprising: Egypt's most famous symbol has left no physical trace.

best_facts.fact: The oldest law about veils, from Assyria, punished slave women for wearing one: they could have their ears cut off.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first veil law was a ban for some women, not a rule for all.

best_facts.fact: The oldest cotton thread in the world survives because copper beads strung on it at Mehrgarh, Balochistan, mineralised it 8,000 years ago.
best_facts.why_surprising: The world's favourite fibre began in South Asia and was preserved by metal.

best_facts.fact: Egyptian kohl contained lead compounds, laurionite and phosgenite, that do not occur naturally and seem to have been made on purpose.
best_facts.why_surprising: Make-up was one of the first chemical industries.

best_facts.fact: Head cones in Egyptian banquet paintings were long thought to be symbols, until two real ones were found on people buried at Amarna, reported in 2019.
best_facts.why_surprising: A 3,000-year-old party accessory was proved real only recently.

best_facts.fact: Tutankhamun owned gloves, including embroidered linen ones, though gloves almost never appear in Egyptian art.
best_facts.why_surprising: The real royal wardrobe had items the art never shows.

best_facts.fact: In Egypt silver was rarer and more valuable than gold, because it had to be imported.
best_facts.why_surprising: It flips our usual ranking of metals.

best_facts.fact: Around 2100 BC, one state office in Girsu, Iraq, oversaw about 6,000 textile workers, mostly women and children, tracked on clay tablets.
best_facts.why_surprising: Industrial-scale clothing production is 4,000 years old.

best_facts.fact: The blue stripes on Tutankhamun's gold mask are glass, not lapis lazuli, and its beard was once glued back on crooked with epoxy, in 2014.
best_facts.why_surprising: The world's most famous artwork has a glass headdress and a repair scandal.

best_facts.fact: Hatshepsut, one of Egypt's most successful rulers, is shown in later statues wearing the king's false beard.
best_facts.why_surprising: Royal dress described the office, not the body.

best_facts.fact: Herodotus wrote that Egyptian priests shaved their entire bodies every other day.
best_facts.why_surprising: Purity rules extended to every hair.

best_facts.fact: The famous red Egyptian split-toe socks date from around AD 300 to 500, three thousand years after the pyramids.
best_facts.why_surprising: Most people assume they are pharaonic.

best_facts.fact: Taram-Kubi, a woman in Ashur around 1900 BC, wove cloth that her husband sold 1,000 km away in Anatolia for silver, and their letters survive.
best_facts.why_surprising: A long-distance family textile business is documented in clay.

best_facts.fact: Every Babylonian man, says Herodotus, carried a seal and a walking stick topped with a carved apple, rose, lily or eagle.
Egyptian children usually wore no clothes at all until about the age of six.
best_facts.why_surprising: Dress started at school age, not birth.

side_dish.title: Writing was invented to count sheep and cloth
side_dish.body_md:
If you want to know why clothing mattered so much in Mesopotamia, look at what the first writing was for. The oldest tablets, about 5,000 of them, mostly from **Uruk** and dated about 3350 to 3000 BC, are not poems, prayers or laws. About **85 per cent** are **accounts**: barley, beer, **sheep** and workers' rations moving in and out of temple stores, counted and checked by officials. Most of the rest are lists of signs, and the lists of manufactured goods already include words for cloth.

The archaeologist **Denise Schmandt-Besserat** argued that writing grew out of an older system of small clay **tokens**, cones, spheres and discs, each standing for a quantity of a good. Officials sealed tokens inside clay envelopes as receipts, then began pressing the tokens into the outside so they could see what was inside without breaking it. From there it was a short step to drawing the signs on flat clay and dropping the tokens altogether. Critics point out that token shapes vary a lot and some common goods, like sheep, have few tokens, so the details are debated. But the basic point is widely accepted: **writing began as bookkeeping**.

That explains the extraordinary paperwork you met today. The 6,000 weavers of Girsu, the Kültepe letters about cloth and silver, the ration lists in wool: these are the same tradition grown up. In Mesopotamia, the hand that wrote and the hand that wove were tied together from the start. A sheep was wealth, its wool was cloth, cloth was wages, and wages had to be written down. Next time you see a cuneiform tablet in a museum, the odds are good it is about something very ordinary, like a delivery of wool.

offline_task.title: Wrap yourself in 3000 BC
offline_task.body_md:
You need one rectangle of cloth: a bedsheet, a dupatta, a dhoti or a long towel. No pins, no scissors. Spend ten minutes trying the three basic ancient wraps.

1. **The Egyptian shendyt.** Wrap the cloth once around your hips, overlapping at the front, and tuck the end in at the waist. Fold a few pleats into the front edge before tucking. Walk, sit cross-legged like the Seated Scribe, and notice how the length changes what you can do.
2. **The Sumerian shawl robe.** Hold one end at your left hip, wrap round your body under your right arm, then up across your chest and over your **left shoulder**, letting the end hang behind. Your right arm and shoulder are now free, as on Gudea and the Priest-King.
3. **The Assyrian spiral.** Start at the ankles and wrap upward in a spiral, so the edge forms diagonal lines, as on Ashurnasirpal's reliefs.

Then ask: which one would you choose to work in, in 40 degree heat? Which one marks you as important? Write one line about each. That is what ancient dress was: a rectangle, a climate, and a message.
